title: Test-Time Adaptation for LLM Agents via Environment Interaction
one_liner: When an AI agent enters a new website or tool environment it does not know, two lightweight tricks at deploy-time teach it the layout and the rules without retraining.
lead: An AI agent trained on general knowledge fails when it meets a new website or set of tools because it does not know that website's button layout or how clicking a button changes the page. This paper adds two simple fix-as-you-go tricks that learn the specific layout and rules during the first few interactions, without needing to retrain the whole model or collect labeled examples.

problem.h2: The agent walks into a new building but reads the old map
paras: An AI agent is trained on millions of web pages and tool examples. But when deployed on a new website or tool system it has never seen, it fails. The website buttons work differently, the page layout is unusual, and the buttons trigger unexpected results. The agent was never trained on this specific website, so its learned instincts do not match what actually happens.

A naive fix is to show the agent many labeled examples from the new website and retrain it. But collecting these examples by hand is expensive and slow. A smarter fix would learn the new website's quirks instantly during deployment, just by trying a few actions and watching what happens.

callout.html: Agents fail on unfamiliar environments because they were not trained on that environment's specific syntax and dynamics.

steps.text: Agent sees an unexpected button response; action did not work as trained.
Measure how badly the model predicted the actual observation in the new environment.
One small adjustment step nudges a list of numbers that shifts the output higher for actions that actually worked.
Use the nudged weights to re-score the next action more accurately.
Before real tasks, ask probe questions and collect a world model in context.

paras: The paper changes two things: First, it adds a tiny learned bias (just a list of small adjustments) that shifts what actions the model thinks are most likely, so they match the new environment's syntax. Second, it collects a small in-context world model by exploring the environment before the real task starts. Both changes happen only at deploy-time, with zero retraining.
object.object: the model's output bias and world model

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: output probability mismatch
hidden.name: how far the model's predicted actions stray from the real environment
paras: The core problem is a hidden mismatch: the model's learned priors (what button it expects to exist or what a click will do) no longer match this new environment. The paper measures this by computing language modeling loss on the current context — how badly does the model predict what actually just happened? A high loss means the model's output probabilities are far from the true responses.

Syntactic alignment uses this loss to update the tiny adaptation bias one step at a time. Dynamics grounding builds an in-context summary of state transitions to fill in the semantic gap. Both are trying to shrink the mismatch between what the model was trained on and what the environment actually does.

heat.caption: Darker means a larger mismatch between what the agent expected and what the environment did

reads.html: The mismatch is the gap between the model's pre-trained guesses about what buttons and pages do, and what actually happens in this new environment.

The paper formulates the test-time input as a context (just a list of numbers representing task instruction, current observation, and history of past actions). The loss on this context measures prediction error on the environment's actual responses.

paras: The trick has two parts. Syntactic alignment fixes the easy part: when the agent observes an unexpected button result, it computes the language modeling loss on that observation. This loss tells it how badly the model's predicted action probabilities misaligned. One small adjustment step nudges a tiny bias that sits before the final output layer. This bias is not retrained weights, just an additive tweak to the hidden representations. The tweaked representations push the output probabilities higher for actions that actually work in this environment.

Dynamics grounding fixes the hard part: the agent does not truly know what each action does. So before the real task, it runs an exploration phase with persona-driven probe questions (pretending to be a user exploring the site). It collects these responses into an in-context summary that the model can reference. Now when planning a multi-step sequence, the model has a crude world model built from real observations, not just guesses from pre-training.

math.words: The model's output scores are shifted by adding a small learned bias to the hidden layer, then projecting to action scores.
math.equation: scores_adapted = (H + delta) * W_out, where delta is updated as: delta := delta - lr * grad_H(L_lm(I))
symbols: the final hidden representation from the model, a list of numbers
the tiny adaptation bias we learn, a list of adjustments same length as H
the final projection matrix that turns hidden numbers into action scores
language modeling loss on the current context I
the slope showing which direction reduces the loss
learning rate, how big each step adjustment is

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Before adaptation: logits for click(Go) = 0.8, click(Search) = 2.1 (model prefers Search)
Environment actually showed date confirmation after Go; loss for predicting that is high
Gradient says: delta should nudge hidden layer toward patterns matching true response
After one step: delta learned delta = [0.05, -0.1, 0.03, ...] (small numbers)
Adapted logits for click(Go) = (H + delta) * W_out = 2.2, click(Search) = 1.5 (now Go ranks first)
Next step, model outputs click(Go), which actually works in this environment

math.note: The same small adaptation bias is applied every step, gently shifting the model's output probabilities to match this one environment.

items.html: If the environment is vast and the probe questions do not cover critical dynamics, the in-context world model stays incomplete. The agent still misses key state transitions.
If early observations are atypical or adversarial, the adjustment step may update the bias in a wrong direction. One bad interaction corrupts the bias for future steps.
Some failures are both syntactic (unexpected button name) and semantic (button does something unexpected). A single adaptation bias may not disentangle them.
When the environment's dynamics are learnable from interaction and the adaptation bias is updated carefully with small step sizes, the agent rapidly aligns and succeeds.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple web-scraping agent that navigates two different mock e-commerce sites with intentionally different button layouts and state transitions. Site A uses button text click(Search), Site B uses click(Go). Each button does something slightly different after clicking (A shows results, B opens a date picker). Measure success rate on a multi-step task like adding an item to cart without adaptation, then with syntactic alignment only, then with both syntactic alignment and a tiny dynamics grounding phase.
demo.metric_eq: success_rate = (tasks completed correctly) / (total tasks attempted); report before and after adaptation.
demo.closing: The demo must show that even two simple adaptations let a generic agent navigate unfamiliar websites without retraining.
